comparator.name: Marine Sciences
comparator.sourceNotes: Current BMS handbook: 135 EC compulsory taught study, 3 EC restricted mathematics/statistics choice, 12 EC thesis and 30 EC open electives. Use one generic pathway, without a named track. MAT14803 is the first-listed restricted option, suitable for the stated Mathematics A preparation; it precedes MAT15103. MAT15403 assumes active high-school statistics or MAT15303. Complete all 138 prescribed taught credits, including all 60 first-year credits and MAE21306, before the thesis; this exceeds the 102-credit minimum. Complete the BC&PL portfolio and coordinator/adviser knowledge check. General, laboratory and fieldwork safety are additional zero-credit obligations, not invented EC. Formal entry rules are distinguished from advisory assumed-knowledge references; renamed mathematics references in MAE21306 are not additional credits.
components: Boundary Crossing and Personal Leadership in Marine Sciences
The 3-credit course includes a core and a learning ribbon across six required courses, ending during the thesis. Passing its portfolio is required for the thesis grade; these are not extra credits.
Global Water Systems and Climate Change
Research Methodology for Human Environment Interactions

Integrated marine field research includes intertidal sampling, sediment transport, fish ecology and observations of Wadden Sea uses. Laboratory and fieldwork safety are required; BMS students have admission priority.
Introduction to Law for the Life and Social Sciences
Global Marine Compounds, Flows, and Cycles
Life History and Biology of Aquatic Animals
Evaluation and Design of Marine Nature-Based Solutions
Research design, marine sampling and monitoring, data analysis and a multi-day overseas field practical. Laboratory and fieldwork safety are required.
Assessment of Marine Nature Based Solutions

Three-credit restricted choice between Mathematics Applied: Introduction and Statistics 1. This example takes the first-listed Mathematics Applied: Introduction, for a student with Mathematics A preparation; it precedes Mathematics Applied: Analysis. Statistics 2 assumes active high-school statistics or Statistics 1.

Required 12-credit individual research thesis, with a proposal, research, report, presentation and defence. Entry requires at least 102 programme credits, all 60 first-year credits and Research Methods for Marine Sciences; the coordinator checks preparation with the study adviser. The boundary-crossing and personal-leadership portfolio must also pass.
Thirty open credits can be used for a minor and/or individual electives. No particular minor, placement or specialist package is assumed.

alternatives.label: Marine ecosystems, coasts & environmental governance
alternatives.labelReason: Combines marine ecology and biological foundations with water and chemical processes, geospatial research, food-system sustainability, economics, law and environmental governance. It connects ecological evidence with decisions about coastal environments and marine resources.
alternatives.concept: Combines marine ecology and biological foundations with water and chemical processes, geospatial research, food-system sustainability, economics, law and environmental governance. It connects ecological evidence with decisions about coastal environments and marine resources.
progression: Every formal prerequisite precedes its dependent course and each assigned term is planned. Research in a Sustainable Delta has no prerequisite and is only planned in the first term; its partner-defined project is not guaranteed marine fieldwork. Biology, chemistry, methods and ecological foundations support later laboratory, marine, geochemical and analytical study. Each plan has 24 unique courses, four per term, Year-1 PPD and at least six 300-level courses.
alternatives.distinctness: The integrated response combines ecology, laboratory foundations, food-system appraisal and coastal processes with legal, social, economic and governance inquiry. It differs by 9 courses from the biological route and 8 from the coastal-systems route.

alternatives.label: Marine biology, ecology & conservation

core: Marine socio-ecological systems, ocean life and biodiversity
Marine ecology, aquaculture, food systems and conservation
Ocean, coastal and climate processes, energy and nature-based solutions
Marine economics, governance, law, policy and dependent communities
Fieldwork, geo-information, modelling, data analysis and independent marine research
adjacent: Ocean climate, coastal systems and offshore energy
questions: How can marine ecosystems be conserved while oceans support food, energy and livelihoods?
How can climate, coastal and spatial evidence guide sustainable ocean decisions?

candidates.label: Coastal climate, spatial evidence & sustainable systems

selection.assessment: The closest response materially addresses marine ecological systems and their coastal, food-production, social and governance connections through actual UCR content. Only after accepting it, the biological conservation concept is accepted with evolution, molecular/biochemical study and quantitative investigation. Only then the coastal climate/spatial/energy concept is accepted with physical systems, data and intervention appraisal. All pass qualitative distinctness and the pairwise floor. Stop at the three-alternative maximum. Dedicated aquaculture, marine organismal field training, advanced ocean circulation and a required marine thesis remain limitations.

trace: Direct organismal diversity, phylogeny, identification and biodiversity measurement support marine-life and conservation inquiry; the survey spans terrestrial and aquatic life rather than reproducing a marine dissection/field sequence.

Complementary supply/demand, incentives, strategic interaction, production and market allocation provide economic foundations for competing ocean uses; macroeconomic sections do not constitute marine-resource economics.

Direct applied sustainability research with a Zeeland partner requires literature review, question/design, investigation and a final product. The project supplies research practice; its subject and methods depend on the partner, so marine field sampling is not guaranteed.

Direct empirical design, sampling, measurement, inference and regression in R support reliable investigation of environmental and social questions; the research project does not guarantee a marine topic.

Direct conservation reasoning about fragmentation, overharvesting, invasive species, climate pressure and species protection supports assessing threats and conservation responses in marine ecosystems.

Direct social-movement theory, environmental justice and Environmental Justice Atlas cases support analysing contested resource use, distributional harm and civic responses; marine policy specialization is not asserted.
Direct population and community ecology, food webs, energy/matter fluxes and ecological modelling in R provide mechanisms for understanding marine ecosystems and conservation effects.

Complementary chemical equilibria, ocean acidification, nutrient cycles, thermodynamics and simple dynamic models supply natural-science tools for analysing marine environmental pressures; this is not an economic or legal course.

Complementary cell structure, metabolism, DNA/heredity, gene expression and biotechnology establish biological foundations for marine-organism and molecular study; no marine field content is asserted.

Complementary sedimentation, geomorphology, geological history and Earth-system/climate interactions explain physical settings and land-to-sea processes relevant to coastal change; it is not advanced physical oceanography.
Direct R-based cleaning, integration, visualisation and exploration of tabular, textual and geospatial data support transparent analysis of environmental and social evidence.

Complementary wave physics, optical spectroscopy, chemical analysis, material structure and evidence appraisal support environmental observation and material/energy reasoning; it is the formal foundation for later remediation and renewable-system study.

Direct microbial culture, microscopy, DNA/PCR, protein purification and reproducible laboratory reporting supply experimental life-science methods for biological inquiry; marine sampling and organismal fieldwork remain separate gaps.
Direct ArcGIS spatial data, projections, surface analysis, remote-sensing/image processing and a geospatial case study support spatial evidence for coastal and environmental decisions.

Direct qualitative design, interviewing, observation, reflexivity, coding and team research support inquiry into marine-dependent communities, stakeholders and institutions; no marine case is guaranteed.

Direct marine ecology and physical/chemical oceanography connect production, microbial processes, estuaries, shores, reefs and deep/polar seas with fisheries, aquaculture, acidification and plastic pollution.

Direct carbonate/redox chemistry, ocean acidification, nutrients/minerals, contaminants and geochemical modelling support water/compound-cycle and pollution analysis; ocean circulation and sediment transport are not fully reproduced.
Direct design of nature-based infrastructure and ecological connectivity across sandy/muddy coasts, rivers, estuaries and ports materially supports marine/coastal nature-based interventions.

Direct legal systems, public/private/international law, case-law analysis and legal argument support understanding institutional rules and rights relevant to ocean use; it does not provide a full maritime-law sequence.

Direct appraisal of food-production systems, biodiversity impacts and farming innovations, including aquaculture, supports the food/environment connection. The course is broadly agricultural and does not replace a specialist marine-food or aquaculture sequence.

Direct Zeeland delta inquiry connects sea-level rise, salinisation, flood/freshwater management, law and ecological trade-offs; evaluating engineered and nature-based responses supports coastal adaptation appraisal.

Direct institutions, common-pool resources, participation, stakeholder analysis and policy evaluation in food/water/energy/climate support environmental resource governance; the Zeeland case is not guaranteed ocean governance.

Direct regression estimators, causal/predictive inference, specification tests and an empirical paper provide tools for analysing economic relationships and evaluating resource policies, not a dedicated marine-economics course.
Direct calculus, differential equations, numerical integration and dynamic-model implementation provide mathematical tools for ecological and environmental modelling.

Direct geoscience risk and adaptation tools, climate-driven hazards, droughts, mining disasters and toxic algal blooms support assessing environmental/coastal risk within the scope of its official description.

Complementary enzymes, biomolecular function, respiration and energy/lipid/nitrogen metabolism support the biological mechanisms underlying organismal growth and production. This is biochemistry, not aquatic-animal physiology or aquaculture management.
Direct climate feedbacks, sea-level rise, ocean acidification and ecosystem impacts connect physical pressures with mitigation, adaptation, justice and stakeholder communication.

Direct molecular cell structure, proteins, membranes, gene expression, signalling and energy processes support the cellular dimension of marine life. The literature project is biomedical, not a guaranteed marine investigation.

Direct soils, shallow aquifers, salinisation, freshwater interventions, field sampling and geophysical surveys support understanding land-water and coastal-groundwater conditions, not open-ocean circulation.

Direct natural selection, population genetics, adaptation, speciation and phylogeny support explaining marine biodiversity and evolutionary responses; this is evolutionary training across organisms, not aquatic life-history specialization.

Direct probability distributions, estimation, hypothesis tests, Bayesian reasoning and Monte Carlo methods support rigorous quantitative ecological research; this is mathematical statistics rather than a marine-methods field course.

Direct Earth-system interactions, system modelling, proxies and isotope tracers support climate reconstruction and environmental-flow reasoning within the official description; no detailed marine-current model is claimed.

Direct market failure, public goods, externalities, collective choice and efficiency/equity analysis support evaluating public intervention and competing uses of marine resources; applications are broader than the marine domain.

Complementary solar-panel/e-waste recycling, metal recovery and soil remediation provide chemical/laboratory tools for appraising resource and pollution consequences of sustainability interventions; this is not marine remediation or offshore design.

Direct regression/classification, model validation, prediction and unsupervised learning support the data-science part of analysing environmental systems; this does not reproduce coupled physical/social marine simulation.

Direct technical/economic appraisal of energy use and solar, wind and bioenergy alternatives supports sustainable-energy decisions. Its company project does not guarantee offshore wind, marine engineering or a coastal topic.
blocks: Shared evolutionary genetics, variation, selection and adaptation form a direct substantive relationship; the scope and credit weights differ.
Shared population/community ecology, food webs and ecosystem processes provide a direct ecological foundation.
Shared marine and estuarine organisms, habitats, ecological processes and human pressures; WUR additionally includes specific field practicals and excursions.

Both examine environmental effects and sustainability of biological food-production systems, including aquaculture. UCR is predominantly comparative farming; WUR integrates seafood supply, trade and governance.
Both substantively address molecular/cellular organisation, membranes, signalling and regulation. WUR includes its own laboratory applications.

The selected general biodiversity survey does not adequately reproduce this dedicated marine-organism adaptation, dissection and intertidal-field component. The strongest marine course already represents Marine Ecology; preserve this distinct specialist gap.

Shared water/compound chemistry, carbonate and nutrient/contaminant processes support part of the flows-and-cycles component. Ocean currents, tides, sediment transport and integrated marine socio-economics are additional WUR scope.
Both develop nature-based coastal/water interventions that combine ecosystem function with human goals; WUR uses a dedicated marine evaluation/design framework and design pitch.

Shared appraisal of coastal/delta water responses, ecological effects and trade-offs directly addresses part of nature-based-solution assessment. WUR adds modelled scenarios and integrated ecosystem-service reports.
Shared climate impacts, sea-level rise and adaptation/mitigation connect climate to water and marine systems; WUR adds explicit hydrological flows and a marine-case systems analysis.
Market failure, externalities, public goods and policy appraisal are substantive shared economic tools. WUR applies resource-economics concepts to fisheries, conservation and competing ocean uses.
Shared legal systems, legal reasoning and case-law analysis provide a meaningful introductory law relationship; WUR focuses on rules and scientific evidence for life/marine sciences.
Both directly analyse institutions, resource users, participation and policy at multiple scales. WUR dedicates the component to ocean/coastal governance.
Spatial evidence, research, modelling & open study
Shared inference, hypothesis tests and regression are specific statistical content, with different mathematical depth and applications.
Shared research design and qualitative sampling/interview/observation methods support human-environment inquiry. WUR specifically develops a complete research proposal and combines strategies.
Shared differentiation, integration and differential equations provide direct mathematical content; the UCR course includes additional modelling and computational work.

Shared statistical model fitting, classification, validation and data-science analysis address a specific part of WUR modelling. UCR does not reproduce coupled ecosystem, economic and spatial simulation.
Shared geospatial data, projections, queries, transformations, terrain/surface analysis and remote sensing provide a direct GIS relationship.

notes.text: WUR combines marine and coastal field research, aquatic-animal biology, aquaculture, ocean processes, marine governance and a required marine thesis. UCR offers a related combination of marine biology, ecology, environmental science, spatial/data methods and governance. It does not reproduce WUR’s full specialist marine sequence, dedicated field methods or aquaculture training.

audience.programmeDescription: Marine Sciences studies oceans, seas and coasts as linked ecological, physical and social systems. WUR combines marine biology and food systems with climate, economics, governance, spatial methods and the design of sustainable solutions.
audience.comparisonExplanation: These UCR programmes approach marine and coastal questions through different combinations of biology, environmental science, data, economics and governance. WUR offers a more extensive specialist marine sequence, including dedicated field courses, aquatic-animal and aquaculture study, ocean processes and a required marine thesis. UCR’s optional independent research is additional to the illustrated 180 credits; a marine project is not guaranteed.
